newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks seen extending gains in coming week.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks seen extending gains in coming week.

text.p: After a week in which the FTSE 100 index of leading British stocks hit a succession of record highs, pundits on Friday said the market may extend its gains into uncharted territory in coming sessions.
Granted, some short-term consolidation may be order.

Yet assuming no external upset such as a sharp fall on Wall Street, they said shares in London should continue to be well supported by the conjunction of positive factors that boosted the market in the past week.

Last Thursday's drop in Britain's underlying inflation rate, and the decision to leave interest rates unchanged, created a positive investment environment that dealers and fund managers said could last for some time yet.
In the very short term shares could come off the boil, but with Wall Street continuing to make progress, the momentum should carry stocks still higher on this side of the Atlantic.
"The FTSE is slightly overbought short-term but it is still looking bullish," said Richard Marshall, an director at Investment Research of Cambridge, a specialist research house.
"After a bit of consolidation it is looking likely to move on to 4,300, which is the next round figure."
On Friday the FTSE 100 closed 10.2 points higher at 4,207.7, its third record close of the week, putting it 151.1 points or 3.7 percent up on last Friday's close.
Marshall said the gains of the past week were accompanied by a rise in trading volumes, seen as another bullish signal as investment institutions actively moved cash into the market.
"Volumes have picked up on the breakout," he said, "and that is a bullish sign...there is a lot of cash around that is coming back into the market."

Amid a scarcity of economic indicators on both sides of the Atlantic, the key focus next week is likely to be on Wednesday's UK retail sales for December. Analysts expect the annual rate of increase to dip to 3.8 percent from 3.9 percent a month before.
A lower-than-expected retail sales figure would be taken as confirmation of Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's judgement in leaving rates unchanged this week and could give markets a further lift.
In the U.S. next week there is a lack of major economic to disturb the picture of steady non-inflationary growth that has helped buoy the Dow in recent sessions.

And despite recent falls in U.S. Treasury bonds -- which set a benchmark for world markets and could be taken as a warning of an impending rate rise -- some see little threat to further stock market progress.
"I can't see anything to destabilise the trend in coming weeks," said Savvas Savouri, Credit Lyonnais Laing strategist.

"There were one or two banana skins still around but we seem to have survived them," Savouri said. "Worries over the rising pound and politics have come and gone and the Dow is giving us momentum. Wall Street seems to have weathered the end-of-year concerns amd so have we."

Yet as the end of January nears, markets on both sides of the Atlantic may begin to focus on the February 4 meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve -- the world's most powerful central bank -- which could yet spook markets with a rate hike.

And with the UK market still to face the political uncertainties guaranteed to come with the start of an election campaign, some pundits believe the FTSE will do well to rise through 4,300 in the medium term. "If the FTSE got to 4,300 or 4,350," said Michael Beggs, fund manager at investment house Guinness Flight, "it would be time to run for cover."
